h1: Grisette: the light farmhouse ale made for hot weather
title: Grisette: The Light Farmhouse Ale | Craft Beer School
desc: What grisette is, where the light Belgian farmhouse ale came from, how it differs from saison and how to brew a 20 litre batch for hot weather.
teaser: A low strength, dry, wheat based cousin of saison. Built for thirsty workers, ideal for an Indian summer.
standfirst: Grisette is a small, light farmhouse ale from Belgium's Hainaut province. It is lower in alcohol than most saisons, dry and refreshing. Here is what we know about it and how to brew one at home.
sections:
Grisette is usually traced to the coal mining region of Hainaut in southern Belgium. The story is that it was brewed as a light, refreshing beer for miners, as saison was for farm workers. The name is often linked to the grey clothing of local factory girls, though origins are hard to confirm.

Its history is patchy. Few records describe exact recipes. The style largely disappeared in the 20th century. Modern craft brewers revived it based on what was known: low strength, a portion of wheat, dry and hoppy. Some competition style guidelines now list it as a style of its own.

A grisette is light and pale, usually 3.5 to 5% ABV. It tastes of soft grain and wheat, with light fruity and spicy esters from farmhouse yeast. Hops add floral or herbal character and a moderate bitterness. The finish is very dry and highly carbonated, which keeps it refreshing.

Compared with a saison, a grisette is lighter in alcohol and body, with less intense yeast character. Compared with a session IPA, it is less hoppy and more about yeast and grain.

Grisette was designed to refresh workers, so it is light, dry and fizzy. Low alcohol makes it easy to drink in heat without feeling heavy. Farmhouse yeast also likes warmer temperatures, often 24 to 30 °C, which makes fermentation easier in India without an elaborate cooling setup.

For anyone looking for lower alcohol craft beer, grisette offers flavour without strength.

For about 20 litres into the fermenter at 75% efficiency, aiming for an OG near 1.038:

  • Pilsner malt: 2.40 kg (70.6%)
  • Wheat malt: 0.85 kg (25.0%)
  • Flaked oats: 0.15 kg (4.4%)

Total grain is 3.4 kg. Mash at 63 to 64 °C for 60 minutes to produce a highly fermentable wort. Use soft water with a little calcium chloride and gypsum in balance.

Hops: bitter to about 25 IBU with a clean variety, then add Saaz, Styrian Goldings or East Kent Goldings late in the boil for aroma. Ferment with a saison or farmhouse yeast, pitching at about 20 °C and letting it rise to 24 to 28 °C. Expect a final gravity near 1.004, giving about 4.4% ABV. Carbonate to around 2.8 to 3 volumes of CO2, using bottles rated for that pressure.

• Stalled fermentation. Some saison strains slow near the end. Keep the temperature up and give it time.
  • Too much spice or phenol. Pitch healthy yeast and avoid extreme temperatures above 30 °C early in fermentation.
  • Thin body. Grisette is light by design, but oats and wheat give enough body to avoid wateriness.
  • Gushing bottles. Highly attenuative yeast can keep working in the bottle. Make sure gravity is stable before bottling.

Because the historical record is thin, brewers interpret grisette freely. A few variations work well:

  • Dry hopped. A light dry hop of 1 to 2 g per litre with a floral or citrus variety lifts the aroma without making it an IPA.
  • Kveik fermented. Norwegian farmhouse yeasts ferment cleanly at 30 to 35 °C, which suits Indian summers. They give a different fruit profile from saison yeast, so treat the result as a cousin rather than a copy. Our guide to kveik yeast for hot climates explains how to use them.
  • A touch of spelt or rye. Swapping part of the wheat for spelt or rye adds a little earthiness or spice.
  • Brettanomyces in the bottle. Some brewers add Brett at bottling for a drier, more rustic finish over months. Only try this with strong bottles and patience.

Change one thing at a time so you know what each variation did.

Grisette is excellent with light food: salads, fish, chicken, vegetable dishes and fresh cheese. In India, try it with a South Indian meal, steamed fish in banana leaf, sprouts chaat or grilled vegetables. Its dry finish and carbonation cut through oil without overpowering delicate flavours.

Historical styles like grisette leave room for interpretation. That freedom is fun but requires judgement. Understanding farmhouse yeast, how wheat and oats affect body and how dryness changes perceived bitterness helps you design a beer that is true to the spirit of the style. Studying style families together, rather than one at a time, makes those choices clearer.
faqs: What is the difference between grisette and saison?
Grisette is lower in alcohol and lighter in body, with milder yeast character. Saison is usually stronger and more complex.
What yeast should I use for grisette?
A saison or farmhouse ale yeast. It gives fruity and spicy notes and ferments well at warmer temperatures.
Usually 3.5 to 5% ABV, making it a light, refreshing beer.
